# R ## R -- Software for statistical computing
**R** can be downloaded [here](https://www.r-project.org):
You can use the graphical user interface that comes with **R**, or you can run **R** through a system like **ESS+emacs** or **RStudio** ()\
Most people use **RStudio** these days ## RStudio ![](figs/rstudio-no-script.PNG){.framed-img fig-align="center" width="90%"} ## RStudio To create a new script, click: `File > New File > R Script` ![](figs/rstudio-open-script.png){.framed-img fig-align="center" width="60%"} Save your script using: `File > Save As` ## RStudio ![](figs/rstudio-script-graphics.png){.framed-img fig-align="center" width="90%"} ## Reproducing the Excel exercise ::: {style="font-size: 80%;"} Create an object called [`year`]{style="background-color: inlinecolor"} to hold the sequence of years. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} year <- 1950:1961 # A vector of integers year # Type the name of an object to see its values ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1950 1951 1952 1953 1954 1955 1956 1957 1958 1959 1960 1961 ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Note that you can use [`seq`]{style="background-color: inlinecolor"} to create sequences in a more general way. The [`c`]{style="background-color: inlinecolor"} function combines two or more vectors. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} updown <- c(seq(from=20, to=100, by=20), seq(from=100, to=20, by=-20)) updown # Two sequences, combined ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 20 40 60 80 100 100 80 60 40 20 ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Use the `length` function to determine the number of values in a vector. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nYears <- length(year) nYears ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 12 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## A simple population model ::: {style="font-size: 80%;"} Create an empty vector to store the data on females. Set female abundance to 100 in the first year. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} females <- rep(NA, nYears) females[] <- 100 ``` :::
::: {.fragment} Use a "for loop" to compute female abundance in subsequent years. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} for(t in 2:nYears) { females[] <- females[] + females[]*0.01 } ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} [**We will use "for loops" for almost every population model that we implement in R**]{.alert .center} ::: ::: ## A simple population model ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='40%'} Generate the data on males using a single line of code. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} males <- females*0.8 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width='60%'} Put the objects in a `data.frame` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} model1 <- data.frame(year, females, males) model1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` year females males 1 1950 111.5668 89.25347 2 1951 111.5668 89.25347 3 1952 111.5668 89.25347 4 1953 111.5668 89.25347 5 1954 111.5668 89.25347 6 1955 111.5668 89.25347 7 1956 111.5668 89.25347 8 1957 111.5668 89.25347 9 1958 111.5668 89.25347 10 1959 111.5668 89.25347 11 1960 111.5668 89.25347 12 1961 111.5668 89.25347 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Graphics ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(females ~ year, data=model1, type="o", xlab="Year", ylab="Abundance", lwd=2, pch=16, ylim=c(0, 120)) lines(males ~ year, data=model1, type="o", col="blue", lwd=2, pch=16) legend(x=1950, y=40, legend=c("Females", "Males"), col=c("black", "blue"), lty=1, pch=16) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab-Excel-R-Basics_files/figure-revealjs/plot-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672} ::: ::: ## Assignment ::: {style="font-size: 65%;"} 1. Create an Excel file and name it "Yourlastname_Yourfirstname". 2. Create the sheet shown on the next page using the techniques covered in this lab. - Use auto-fill to create the first two columns. - For the "Adults" column, use the equation shown for cells C3 through C22. Note: For cell C2, you can directly enter the value "10". 3. Copy "Sheet1" to a new sheet and change the color and thickness of the lines. You can pick any colors and thicknesses you want. 4. Replicate steps 1--3 using a "for loop" in a self-contained R script. Note that you will need code to create both graphs---the original one and the one with the new line color and thickness. - Hint: You can make the juveniles data using [`seq`]{style="background-color: inlinecolor"} and [`c`]{style="background-color: inlinecolor"}, like we did with the [`updown`]{style="background-color: inlinecolor"} example earlier. 5. Upload the Excel workbook (with both sheets) and the R script to ELC by 5:00pm on Friday. Always clear your RStudio workspace and then rerun the R script before submitting it to ELC. :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
